column1: What is the foundational invariant of precision layout in hand-tool woodworking?
column2: Every measurement is a comparison, not an objective truth; errors accumulate and compound across a layout sequence, so workflow must be designed to cancel errors rather than let them stack.

column1: Why must every layout tool register against the face side and face edge of a board?
column2: This is a topological discipline that quarantines dimensional errors (cup, hollow, etc.) to surfaces you've deliberately excluded from reference, ensuring all subsequent measurements trace back to one true surface.

column1: What physical feature does a marking knife create that a pencil line cannot, and why does it matter?
column2: A knife wall severs surface fibers cleanly on the waste side, creating a small triangular trench with an exact near wall—this physically guides chisels and saws, unlike a pencil line which has no registration surface.

column1: What is the central invariant governing hand-saw tooth geometry?
column2: Wood's fiber orientation is constant, and tooth shape, set, file angle, and cutting posture must all be chosen relative to whether the cut is ripping (with grain) or crosscutting (across grain).

column1: How do rip saw and crosscut saw tooth geometries differ mechanically?
column2: Rip saw teeth have a nearly vertical rake angle (~90°) acting like chisels paring along fiber bundles; crosscut teeth first score fibers with a knife-like slicing action before scooping the chip, preventing tear-out.

column1: What is saw 'set' and what happens if it is removed or overdone?
column2: Set is the deliberate lateral displacement of alternating teeth, creating a kerf wider than the plate. Remove it and the saw jams within strokes; too much set causes a wide, ragged kerf and excessive thrust demand.

column1: Why do Japanese pull-stroke saws use thinner blades than Western push-stroke saws?
column2: Pull-stroke saws place the blade under tension rather than compression, allowing a thinner, harder plate with finer teeth and a narrower, cleaner kerf—a structural engineering tradeoff, not just cultural preference.

column1: How do bed angle and primary bevel combine to determine a plane's effective cutting angle?
column2: Effective cutting (attack) angle = bed angle + primary bevel angle. A 45° bed with a 25° bevel yields a 45° cutting angle (common pitch).

column1: Why do figured woods (curly maple, interlocked grain) require higher plane cutting angles (50-60°)?
column2: Higher angles compress fibers before severing them, preventing the blade from diving beneath the surface and tearing out chunks on reversing/interlocked grain—at the cost of increased cutting resistance and force.

column1: What is the fundamental invariant governing wood movement and joinery design?
column2: Wood moves, but joints must not: timber expands/contracts across the grain by up to ~1% width per 4% RH change (negligible along grain), so fastening strategies must accommodate this differential or fail via splitting/shearing.

column1: Why does a brace with a longer sweep arm generate more torque than one with a shorter sweep?
column2: The brace converts hand force into torque via mechanical advantage equal to the ratio of sweep radius to chuck radius; a 10-inch sweep produces roughly ten times the torque of direct hand force on the bit.

column1: In hand-plane cutting mechanics, why does cutting 'against the grain' cause tearout?
column2: The blade fractures fibers below the intended surface as splits propagate ahead of the edge into deeper layers, rather than wedging beneath fibers and lifting them cleanly as occurs when cutting with the grain.
